hints.hint: For puzzles where agents announce ignorance, first write down exactly what each agent knows. If the setup leaves ambiguous which of two quantities was revealed, that ambiguity is part of every agent's uncertainty: do not case-split externally, assume one reading, and restart. An agent holding x who sees N must keep every partner value legal under either reading (sum/product reveal: N-x and N/x when each is a valid natural number). "I do not know" means at least two partner values survive, which constrains that agent's own number. Apply announcements in order, filtering the set left by the previous one. Verify at the end: your candidate makes both announcements true and no rival candidate does. Track eliminations once and move forward instead of relitigating; looping exhausts your budget before you answer.
hints.mutation: replace abstract set-filtering recipe with a concrete first move, the sum/product ambiguity trap, and an anti-looping directive

hints.hint: For root-locus questions, take moduli before hunting individual roots. Given (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n, divide by (z-b)^n and take absolute values: |z-a| = k|z-b| with k = |c|^(1/n). That is an Apollonius circle, so every root lies on one circle whichever n-th root of c you pick; you never need the roots themselves. Avoid parametrizing the ratio as k e^{i t} and eliminating t, which is where sign and algebra slips occur. Instead set z = x+iy, square both sides, collect the x^2+y^2 terms, divide by their coefficient, and complete the square to read off center and radius. Note z = b is never a root, and k = 1 degenerates to a line. Confirm by substituting one real root into your circle equation.
hints.mutation: generalize to Apollonius-modulus method; replace parametrize-and-eliminate step with x+iy complete-the-square

The revision therefore drops the problem-specific substitution scaffolding, states the general modulus/Apollonius-circle framing for any (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n, prescribes the safer x+iy complete-the-square route, and adds the degenerate-case and verification checks.

hints.hint: Covered area = sum of areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Fix coordinates once, with the shared point at the origin, and never re-derive that setup. Key pruning: only the two edges meeting at the shared point can cut the small square; show the far edges are too distant to matter, so the overlap is a right-angle wedge cut by the small square. Then be numeric, not qualitative: for one angle, find where the two rays exit the square, list the polygon vertices in order, and shoelace it. Repeat for a second angle. If the two values match, suspect the overlap is angle-independent and confirm it by pairing congruent pieces under the square's own rotational symmetry; otherwise minimize over the symmetry-reduced range. Box a number well before you run long.

hints.hint:
Several hidden degree-n polynomials must jointly hit prescribed values at consecutive integers. Two traps: do NOT difference one polynomial and conclude impossibility, and do NOT assume each polynomial is used once.

Method: write the prescribed value as a function of the INPUT, not the position; for an arithmetic progression over consecutive inputs the target is affine, L(x)=px+q. Fix one polynomial P and set g=P-L. Every input assigned to P is a root of g. Compare degrees to show g is not identically zero, so g has at most n roots; that caps how many inputs any single polynomial can serve. Multiply/sum that cap over the family for the upper bound, then exhibit a construction giving each polynomial a disjoint block of inputs where it interpolates L. Report one exact integer.
hints.mutation: name the two observed failure traps up front, then give the concrete P-minus-affine-target root-counting recipe
hints.subagent_summary: All 8 rollouts scored 0. Two runs also burned the full token budget oscillating between these two wrong frames. The incumbent hint's abstract 'affine-in-index target' and 'suitable finite difference' language was never operationalized, so the revision states the target as affine in the INPUT, makes g = P - L and its root count the explicit first move, and warns against the exact two traps observed.

hints.hint:
When unknown points on a fixed curve y=g(x) are tied by a known displacement (u,v), reduce to ONE unknown: let the free vertex be (t, g(t)) and its partner (t+u, g(t)+v), then solve the single scalar equation g(t+u) = g(t) + v.

For a logarithmic curve, convert that additive offset to a multiplicative one BEFORE cross-multiplying: log_c(B) - log_c(A) = v means B/A = c^v. Flipping the direction or sign of that power is the dominant failure mode.

If you hit an impossible identity or a negative discriminant, you flipped the offset: recheck only that conversion line. Do not conclude the configuration is impossible, and do not restart from scratch.

Discard roots that reproduce a given vertex (degenerate). Finish with the shoelace determinant in cyclic order.
hints.mutation: replace generic recipe with one-unknown translation setup plus log offset sign trap and no-restart rule

Successful rollouts all did the same thing early: parametrize one vertex, translate it by the displacement, convert the offset multiplicatively, drop the degenerate root, then shoelace. The revised hint front-loads that one-unknown reduction, names the sign/direction trap explicitly, and forbids the restart spiral, while dropping incumbent words spent on parameter fitting that every rollout already did correctly.

hints.hint:
When a random process moves items between stacks, do NOT assume all final arrangements are equally likely, and do NOT assume an item is equally likely to land in any slot. That unjustified-uniformity leap is the trap here; refuse it even if the answer looks elegant.

Instead encode a whole run as a string of move letters (T = source-to-middle, G = middle-to-destination). A string is legal only if it never pops an empty pile. With few items, enumerate all legal strings. Multiply step probabilities along each string: 1/2 when both moves are available, but exactly 1 when only one is. Track the labelled piles to read the true final order, remembering each transfer reverses a pile. Sum probabilities of the strings meeting the asked event, and check all legal strings total 1.

hints.hint: When many weighted power sums sum a_i*(node_i)^k are prescribed, read them as one linear functional L(p) = sum a_i p(node_i) on polynomials p of the node variable; k is p's degree, not an index. Moments vanishing for k=1..N-1 with the k=N moment normalized make L return p's leading coefficient for every p of degree <= N, and the absent k=0 equation forces p(0)=0, so keep a factor x. To isolate ONE weight, choose the monic p vanishing at 0 and at all nodes but that one; then L(p) = weight * p(node), giving the weight as a reciprocal product of node differences. Never expand the Vandermonde system or solve for all weights, and reject any argument concluding the weights are all zero. Watch signs, test the idea on 3 nodes, then stop.

hints.hint: When totals are given for a whole group but the group size N is unknown, treat N as an unknown divisor. A clause like "each item's share is a whole number" forces N to divide every listed total, so N is a common divisor: factor them, take their gcd, and if nothing else pins N down choose the largest admissible divisor, then check each total/N is an integer. Treat decorative layout wording (streets, rows, groups) as a constraint only if it supplies real numbers. Fix the percentage base before computing: "markup is p% of cost" means price = cost x (1 + p/100), not cost/(1 - p/100). Sum components first, divide by N, apply the multiplier last, and keep the original units.

hints.hint: When the constraint is a commuting identity like p(q(x)) = q(p(x)) with unknown coefficients, do not expand the composition: its degree is the product of the degrees, and drowning in that algebra is the main way these problems are lost. Instead posit an affine link q = a*p + b, testing the simplest cases a = ±1 first, and fix b from the given point values. The identity then reduces to "p commutes with an affine involution", which forces p to be antisymmetric about that map's fixed point m: p(m+t) + p(m-t) is constant. Use that symmetry to produce the requested outputs directly instead of solving for every coefficient. Expect one leftover free coefficient; verify the requested values do not depend on it, then set it to something convenient and check the identity numerically at two points.
hints.mutation: give an explicit affine-ansatz first move plus symmetry identity, warn against expanding the composition

hints.hint: Model the whole procedure as one permutation of positions and answer with its order. First, brute-force simulate it on the two smallest sizes, writing out the full position-to-position map, before you propose any formula. Do not shortcut from "each stage is an involution" or "each stage swaps two halves" to a shift or a product of 2-cycles: composing stages in sequence usually creates long cycles, so compute the composition entry by entry, applying stages in the stated order. Then trace one position's forward orbit until it returns, and take the order as the lcm of cycle lengths. Index from 0 and write indices in fixed-width binary to expose a bitwise pattern. If a formula and a simulation disagree, trust the simulation.
